**Validation**
- The engine (engine.py) reproduces trend.run_portfolio / run_vol_targeted exactly for all 5 variants: max abs difference 0 on net, gross, costs and positions.
- On the 82-market universe with a half-day lag and bp costs, v5 reproduces cv_donnees restatement_grid: Sharpe 1.0742 / 0.7235 / 0.3752 vs 1.074 / 0.724 / 0.375.
- L1 reproduces the published figures, all from 1990:

| Variant | CAGR (%) | Sharpe | Vol (%) | Max drawdown (%) | Costs (%/yr) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | 13.03 | 0.50 | 24.59 | −66.85 | 1.29 |
| v2 | 19.34 | 0.92 | 17.63 | −40.23 | 1.41 |
| v3 | 22.28 | 1.03 | 18.27 | −41.38 | 1.70 |
| v4 | 28.08 | 1.13 | 21.18 | −48.43 | 2.15 |
| v5 | 29.60 | 1.17 | 21.43 | −47.79 | 2.46 |

- L1 calendar years 2010–2025 match resultats/rapport_annees.csv with zero difference.

**Definitions**
- **L0:** published 'gross' series plus the full US T-bill.
- **L1:** published 'net' series plus the full US T-bill.
- **L2:**
  - Universe: 82 markets (CUA1 and SCO1 dropped; weights and IDM recomputed).
  - Execution: half-day lag 1.5, held = 0.5·pos(t−1) + 0.5·pos(t−2), with trades booked when executed; the vol-targeting scale is measured on the lagged real-cost P&L.
  - Costs: real IBKR cost of the standard contract, real_bp/1e4 per unit of notional traded. ER4 half-spread corrected to 0.0025, giving 0.339 bp instead of 0.823. Rolls = 2 × cost × rolls/yr.
  - Cash: margin share m_t = min(0.17 × G_t / 8.7837, 1) earns 0 (G_t = gross exposure held that day). The rest earns max(T-bill − 0.5 %, 0).
- **Excess return** = total − T-bill at every level. At L2 it therefore includes the cash shortfall; 'cagr_futures_excess' gives it before the shortfall.
- **Conventions** (as rapport_pdf.py):
  - Cash = previous day's DTB3 × calendar days / 365, from 1990-01-01.
  - CAGR years = days/365.25 + 1/261.
  - Vol = std of daily total × 16; Sharpe = mean/std of daily excess × 16.
  - Costs per year = sum / years.
  - The 2023-07→2026-07 window runs from 2023-07-11 to 2026-07-10 (exactly 3 years).

- Biggest step: dropping the ethanol artefact CUA1 and SCO1, especially since 2010 (−3.2 pts).
- Second: the cash rule (about −0.5 to −1.0 pt/yr). Third: the lag (about −0.7 pt).
- Real costs slightly help, because they are below the bp model.

**L2 sensitivities for v5 (CAGR from 1990 / from 2010, %; base 26.53 / 7.51)**
- Cost fixed in USD per contract, at historical price levels: 24.15 / 7.02. Costs in the 1990s were about twice today's in bp: 4.0 %/yr average over 1990–2026, vs 2.1.
- Real costs ×2: 23.89 / 5.15.
- Margin 23 % instead of 17 %: 26.37 / 7.43.
- Full-day lag: 25.78 / 6.76.

**Calendar-year total returns 2010–2025 (annees.csv)**
- v5 L1: 39.4, −4.2, −11.1, 10.1, 82.3, 10.2, −18.1, −13.5, 2.3, 22.7, 86.4, 36.4, 35.2, −10.6, −14.4, 1.8; 2026 to 10/07: −2.2.
- v5 L2: 28.3, −4.1, −8.3, 1.3, 72.2, 13.7, −20.8, −11.8, 2.9, 14.5, 49.3, 16.2, 33.8, −18.4, −12.0, 6.5; 2026 to 10/07: 0.9.
- The L1 gap in 2020–2021 (86 → 49 and 36 → 16) mostly comes from CUA1.

**Reading**
- Net of all fees and realistic execution, the past still looks good from 1990: L2 CAGR 11–27 %, Sharpe 0.44–1.05.
- From 2010 it is much weaker: L2 CAGR −1.8 to 7.5 %, Sharpe ≤ 0.37.
- From 2015, L2 Sharpe is ≤ 0.22 and CAGR −3.2 to 4.6 %.
- The last 3 years are negative for every variant except v2: −4.3 % to +0.6 %/yr.
- The ranking v5 ≥ v4 > v3 > v2 >> v1 holds at every level over the long periods. It reverses over the last 3 years, when v2 is best.
- Fixed IB Gateway costs (about USD 400/yr) are ignored, as specified. They are negligible at the multi-million scale the L2 full universe implies: ≤ 0.01 %/yr above about USD 4M, but about 0.4 %/yr at USD 100k.

**Scripts:** engine.py, 01_check_engine.py, 02_main.py, 03_decomposition.py, 04_resume.py. Cached series are in series.pkl and runs_published.pkl.

caveats: L2 assumes fractional positions in all 82 markets, as if capital were unlimited. Holding at least 1 standard contract at the median position is only reached in 63 markets at USD 5M, and the strictly retail-accessible universe is only 66 markets (simulation/subsets.csv). L2 is therefore an upper bound for a large account. Smaller accounts (14 / 24 / 40 markets at 100k / 250k / 1M) trade fewer markets and pay micro-contract costs, so they do worse.

L2 applies today's (2026) real costs in bp to the whole history. When prices were lower, costs in bp were higher: with a constant USD cost per contract, v5 costs average 4.0 %/yr over 1990–2026 instead of 2.1 %, and CAGR from 1990 falls from 26.5 % to 24.2 %. Even that is optimistic for the 1990s pit era (higher commissions, wider tick spreads), so L2 figures before about 2005 are flattering.

Real IBKR costs come out below the bp backtest model (v5 2.11 vs 2.46 %/yr) because standard equity, bond and STIR contracts cost well under 1 bp. This does not hold for micro contracts or small accounts. ER4 Euribor is the biggest single cost item (mean |position| about 1.2× capital in v5), so its half-spread correction (0.0072 → 0.0025) matters.

The margin share is approximated as 0.17 × gross exposure / 8.78, proportional to gross notional whatever the asset mix. The exchange initial-margin estimate (23 % for v5) changes CAGR by only about −0.1 to −0.2 pt/yr.

The cash rule uses US T-bill − 0.5 %, floored at 0, as the project uses USD T-bills. The real IBKR USD benchmark is Fed Funds, and a EUR-based investor would earn on €STR. The 'no interest on the first 10k' and pro-rata-below-100k rules are ignored (irrelevant at multi-million scale), as are the IB Gateway fixed costs of about USD 400/yr: ≤ 0.01 %/yr above USD 4M, but about 0.4 %/yr at USD 100k.
Not modelled: market impact or slippage beyond the half-spread, whole-contract rounding, and data errors other than CUA1/SCO1. No tax anywhere.
At L2, 'excess' means total − T-bill, so it includes the cash shortfall; 'cagr_futures_excess' gives the futures excess before the shortfall. Vol is std of daily TOTAL return × 16, as in the project.

The 2023-07→2026-07 window uses returns from 2023-07-11 to 2026-07-10 (exactly 3 years); cv_donnees starts on 2023-07-10, a one-day difference. In this window L2 is above L1 because the dropped CUA1/SCO1 lost money and the lag helped slightly; this is not evidence that live trading beats the backtest.
L0 for the vol-targeted variants (4, 5) uses the published scale, which is computed on net P&L; L0 is the same positions without costs.

These are past backtest results, and variants 3–5 were chosen after seeing the data. The decay is clear: v5 L2 Sharpe is 1.05 from 1990, 0.71 from 2000, 0.37 from 2010, 0.22 from 2015 and negative over the last 3 years. Forward expectations (forward Monte Carlo: v5 central Sharpe 0.20–0.27) are far below the 1990–2026 history and must not be read off these tables.

verification.summary:
The var_passe_global tables are correct: every number reproduces independently. Seven narrative statements in the summary and caveats are wrong or overstated and need rewording. No table needed correcting, and no project file was modified. All verification work is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-snt-2b-adam-cieniewicz/4246b01c-1857-5934-aed2-b3eb85d88a07/scratchpad/audit/verif_var_passe_global/.

**How I checked**
- I wrote my own code (01_runs.py, 02_metrics.py, 03_bridge.py, 04_claims.py, 05_sens.py) without importing engine.py or reading its caches.
- L1 positions come straight from the project's trend.run_portfolio and trend.run_vol_targeted. For L2, I ran trend.run_portfolio on the 82-market subset and rebuilt the vol-targeting scale myself from the lagged, real-cost P&L.
- I re-implemented the half-day lag, the real costs (from the raw fee, half-spread, multiplier, price and FX columns, with the ER4 half-spread set to 0.0025, giving 0.339 bp) and the cash leg (from the raw FRED DTB3 file).

**What matches**
- I ran all 5 variants, not just v2 and v5, at L0, L1 and L2. They match var_passe_global.csv to at most 5e-7 on every metric and period (the file is rounded to 6 decimals). Comparison: compare_var_passe_global.csv.
- annees.csv matches for every (variant, level) to 5e-5. resume_large.csv matches the long file.
- L1 equals the published resultats/rapport_indicateurs.csv for CAGR, Sharpe, vol, max drawdown, costs and exposure. It also equals rapport_cagr_periodes.csv for 2000 and 2010, and rapport_annees.csv for every year from 1990 to 2025.
- The L1→L2 bridge for v2 and v5 (S0 to S4) matches decomposition.csv to 5e-7. The sensitivities for costs ×2, margin 23 % and full-day lag match exactly for v2 and v5.
- S2 for v5 reproduces the cv_donnees restatement grid: Sharpe 1.074 / 0.723 / 0.375.

**Definitions confirmed**
- L2 drops CUA1 and SCO1, with weights and IDM recomputed.
- The half-day lag is applied to both the P&L and the vol-targeting scale.
- Costs are the real per-contract cost of the standard contract at 2026 prices. Rolls are 2 × cost × rolls per year.
- The cash rule is: margin share = min(0.17 × gross exposure ÷ 8.7837, 1) earns 0, and the rest earns max(T-bill − 0.5 %, 0). The 8.7837 is v5's published mean exposure, which I recomputed.
- The cash convention is the previous day's DTB3 × calendar days ÷ 365.
- CAGR is in calendar time, with years = days ÷ 365.25 + 1/261, as in rapport_pdf.py. Vol is the std of daily total return × 16, and Sharpe is mean ÷ std of daily excess × 16.
- The last window runs from 2023-07-11 to 2026-07-10, which is exactly 3 years.
- The IBKR rules on the first 10k and on pro-rata below 100k NAV are ignored, and so are the IB Gateway fixed costs. Both omissions are stated, and they only hold for a large account.

**Narrative statements that need fixing**
1. "ER4 is the largest single cost item for v5" is wrong after the ER4 correction.
   - At L2 from 1990, ER4 costs 0.080 %/yr and ranks 5th.
   - The largest is IR4 (the ASX 90-day bank bill) at 0.134 %/yr, followed by PA1 0.099, NO1 Curncy 0.093 and NG1 0.086.
   - From 2010, IR4 is 0.141 and ER4 0.120.
   - The ER4 correction itself is worth about 0.11 pt/yr of cost.
2. "The 2020–21 L1 gap mostly comes from CUA1" is only half right. In 2020 the gap comes mostly from SCO1 (iron ore); in 2021 mostly from CUA1.
   - 2020: dropping SCO1 alone takes v5 from 86.4 % to 59.6 %. Dropping CUA1 alone gives 79.2 %.
   - 2021: dropping CUA1 alone takes v5 from 36.4 % to 20.7 %. Dropping SCO1 alone gives 29.0 %.
3. "In 2023-07→2026-07, L2 beats L1 partly because the lag helped" is wrong for v5.
   - The lag effect is +0.17 / +0.09 / 0.00 / +0.03 / −0.23 pt for v1 to v5, so essentially nil, and negative for v5.
   - The gap comes from dropping CUA1 and SCO1 (+1.1 to +2.6 pt) and from real costs (+0.1 to +0.2 pt). The cash rule takes back 0.9 to 1.0 pt.
4. "The ranking v5 ≥ v4 > v3 > v2 >> v1 holds at every level over the long periods" fails at L2 from 2015.
   - There v3 is at or above v4: CAGR 4.20 % vs 4.14 %, Sharpe 0.203 vs 0.199.
   - At L1 from 2010, v4 and v5 are tied on Sharpe (0.5412 vs 0.5411).
5. The sensitivity with costs fixed in USD per contract (X1) is mis-described.
   - "1990s costs about twice today's" actually describes the 1990–2026 average: 4.01 vs 2.11 %/yr.
   - By decade, X1 costs are about 3× L2 in the 1990s (6.7 vs 2.2 %/yr), 1.9× in the 2000s (3.5 vs 1.8) and 1.2× from 2010 (2.67 vs 2.21).
   - X1 also uses today's contract sizes, so it is only an order of magnitude.
6. "Standard equity, bond and STIR contracts cost much less than 1 bp" is overstated.
   - Median real cost: equities 0.77 bp, bonds 0.73 bp and FX 0.80 bp, against 1 bp in the model. STIR is 0.37 bp against 0.5 bp.
   - That is about 20–30 % below the model, not "much less".
7. "Average T-bill accrual ≈ 2.8 %/yr" should read 2.72 %/yr (the published money-market CAGR is 2.76 %).

**Remaining approximations, none of which changes the tables**
- The margin share scales with gross exposure, so it falls to 14.4 % for v5 over the last 3 years. The asset-mix margin model in couts/margin_estimate.csv says recent margin is no lower than the long-run average, so the last-3-year cash shortfall may be understated by about 0.1 pt/yr. The 23 % margin sensitivity covers this.
- The cash leg is in USD (T-bill rather than Fed Funds). A EUR-based investor would earn less, especially from 2015 to 2022. That is already listed as a caveat but is not quantified.

Supporting files are claims_check.csv, v5_L2_cost_by_market.csv, v5_drop_one_by_one.csv, compare_bridge.csv and compare_sensitivities.csv.

**Engine check.** veng.py reproduces trend.run_portfolio and trend.run_vol_targeted bit for bit for all 5 variants (max position difference 0, max net difference 0). On the full 84 markets the published Sharpe since 1990 comes out at 0.504 / 0.921 / 1.026 / 1.127 / 1.171, with vol 24.6 / 17.6 / 18.3 / 21.2 / 21.4 % and gross exposure 5.26 / 5.60 / 6.77 / 7.78 / 8.78.

**Market subsets (01_subsets.py, saved in subsets_variantes.csv).** Same rule as the audit: capital/tiers.py greedy round-robin on the strict 66-market retail universe (no CUA1, no SCO1), smallest liquid contract, each variant's own median |position| over 2023-07-10 to 2026-07-10, then the run_all.verified_subset re-run-and-drop loop.
- For variant 5 the greedy and verified subsets are identical to the audit's (14 / 24 / 40 markets).
- Number of markets per variant at 100k / 250k / 1M:
  - v1: 13 / 21 / 36
  - v2: 13 / 21 / 36
  - v3: 14 / 22 / 37
  - v4: 13 / 23 / 38 (3 / 2 / 4 markets dropped after the re-run)
  - v5: 14 / 24 / 40
- Variant 2's median positions are 0.575 times variant 5's (1/1.74), so it fits about 1 to 4 fewer markets per tier.
- The subsets overlap heavily. v3 is a subset of v5 at every tier. v2 differs from v5 by at most 1 to 4 markets; for example v2 at 100k has ER4 in place of CF1 and SFR5.
- Every market holds at least 1.00 contract at its median position. The rule still holds under the half-day-lag system.

**Simulation (02_run.py).**
- Whole contracts with Carver buffering (sim.integer_positions) and today's notional and spreads.
- Real IBKR costs per contract: fee plus half-spread on trades and on rolls, with the ER4 half-spread at 0.0025.
- Capital held fixed; 1999-01-04 to 2026-07-10.
- Headline execution is a half-day lag: P&L = 0.5·pos(t-1)·r + 0.5·pos(t-2)·r, trade costs split half on t and half on t+1. For v4 and v5 the vol-target scale is measured on the lagged P&L.
- IBKR cash leg: margin (audit's flat-k model, 0.25 × σ × |exposure|, computed on each variant × tier's actual contract positions) earns 0. The rest earns max(T-bill − 0.5 %, 0), nothing on the first USD 10k, pro-rata below 100k NAV. IB Gateway fixed cost is USD 400 a year.

**Reconciliation with the audit.** At same-close execution, v5's Sharpe since 2010 is exactly 0.406 / 0.421 / 0.389 (100k / 250k / 1M), and since 2000 it is 0.566 / 0.694 / 0.700. The half-day lag costs v5 between −0.005 and −0.019 of Sharpe and v3 −0.005 to −0.018. For v1, v2 and v4 the effect is −0.02 to +0.02, which is path noise in whole contracts.

caveats: Today's notional mode applies today's contract sizes and spreads (2026-07-10) to the whole history. Micro contracts are assumed to have existed throughout, though most date from 2019 to 2024. Spreads were wider before about 2010, so trading costs for 2000-2010 are probably understated.
Market selection uses positions from 2023-07 to 2026-07 and today's notionals. This is look-ahead in the choice of markets (though not selection on performance), as in the audit.

Capital is held fixed: P&L is a % of C and CAGR compounds those daily returns. A real account would also have to resize contracts as its value changed. At the 100k tier the cash pro-rata below 100k NAV is ignored after drawdowns, which slightly understates the cash shortfall there.

The cash leg uses US T-bill (DTB3) as a proxy for IBKR's USD benchmark, with the rate floored at 0. Margin uses the audit's flat k = 0.25 × max(EWM32, 1-year vol) × |exposure|, computed on each variant × tier's actual contract positions rather than by scaling 17 % by gross exposure. The two methods agree within about 1 point of margin, which is negligible for the shortfall.

The half-day lag is approximated by a 50/50 mix of close-to-close returns. For v4 and v5 the vol-target scale uses the lagged fractional P&L of the system (bp-model costs), not the realised whole-contract P&L.

v1 (fixed amount) does not control risk. On retail subsets it realises 35-39 % vol with drawdowns of -83 to -88 %, so its compounded CAGR is dominated by volatility drag. Its Sharpe since 2010 is about 0 even in the published 84-market backtest (0.07).

With only 13 to 40 markets, short windows depend heavily on which markets are in the subset. For example, over 2023 to 2026 v5 returns +6.0 % excess at 100k but -9.0 % at 250k, mainly because gold is the only metal in the 100k subset. Gold is also an asset the investor already holds, so the 100k result over recent years partly duplicates his existing exposure.

Sharpe and vol use ×16 (project convention); the data have about 261 weekdays a year, so √261 would raise values by about 1 %. CAGR is in calendar time. 'sharpe' is excess return after real trading costs; 'sharpe_all_in' also deducts cash shortfall and fixed costs, measured against the T-bill.

Each series in series_variantes.pkl starts 1999-01-04 and its first day includes the initial trade-in cost. The DataFrame attrs (description, stats) survive pickling; the same stats are also in series_variantes_stats.csv. Gross exposure is inflated by short-rate and Schatz notionals (for example 19.4× for v5 at 250k), so the forward MC should use mean_margin rather than gross exposure to model the cash leg.

verification.summary:
I rebuilt the retail simulation from scratch and it holds up. The numbers in var_passe_retail are right. A few sentences in its summary are wrong or loose, and no data file needs correcting.

My code (verif_var_passe_retail/indep.py plus scripts 00 to 10) uses only the project's trend.py, the raw data, specs.csv and the cost-audit file. It does not import veng.py, sim.py or engine.py. Nothing under /home/user/snt-2b-adam-cieniewicz was modified; git status is clean.

**What I checked and confirmed**
- **Strategy engine:** my positions and net returns are identical to trend.run_portfolio / run_vol_targeted, both on all 84 markets and on the v2 and v5 250k subsets (difference 0). The published 1990+ figures come out exactly: CAGR 13.0 / 19.3 / 22.3 / 28.1 / 29.6 %, Sharpe 0.504 / 0.921 / 1.026 / 1.127 / 1.171.
- **Market subsets:** I re-derived all 15 variant × tier subsets independently (greedy pass, then the re-run-and-drop loop). Every set matches. v5 matches the audit's 14 / 24 / 40 markets, in the same order.
- **At least 1 contract per market:** every subset passes with its own variant's positions. The lowest median is 1.002 contracts (v2 at 1M); with the half-day lag it is 1.006. The median number of whole contracts actually held over 2023-07 to 2026-07 is at least 1 in every market.
- **Contract table:** notional per contract agrees to within 4e-6, cost per side agrees exactly, and Euribor ER4 uses the 0.0025 half-spread. 9 of the 66 markets use the assumed micro-contract costs (USD 1 fee, 1.5 × the standard half-spread).
- **Full simulation:** I re-ran v2 and v5 at 250k, and in fact all 15 keys, both with the half-day lag and with same-close execution. This covers whole contracts, Carver buffering, fees, half-spread, rolls, the IBKR cash rule and USD 400 a year of fixed costs. All metrics agree within 0.0007 percentage points. The daily series agree to within 1e-7, apart from rare single days (at most 2.4e-4) where a rounding exactly at 0.5 flips because specs.csv stores notionals rounded to whole dollars.
- **Same-close v5 Sharpe** equals the audit's ER4-corrected values: 0.566 / 0.694 / 0.700 since 2000 and 0.406 / 0.421 / 0.389 since 2010.
- **No look-ahead in the strategy itself:** I recomputed everything on data cut off at 2008-09-30, 2015-06-30 and 2022-12-30 for v2 250k, v5 250k, v1 100k and v4 1M. Contracts, positions and net returns up to each cut-off are unchanged (difference 0). The only look-ahead is the one already declared: markets are chosen using 2023–2026 positions and today's contract sizes.
- **No tax anywhere:** no tax term appears in the scripts or output columns.

**Corrections to the summary text** (the files themselves are fine)
1. Half-day lag effect on Sharpe: for v1 it is consistently positive, +0.007 to +0.025, so it is not "path noise". For v4 the range is −0.041 to +0.020 (−0.024 to +0.020 over the long windows), not −0.02 to +0.02.
2. The claim that the two margin methods "agree within about 1 point" is wrong. v1's computed margin is 16.6 to 18.4 %, against 9.8 % from scaling 17 % by gross exposure. v5's subsets give 12.4 / 14.2 / 14.7 %, not 17 %; 16.8 % only holds on all 84 markets. The effect on the cash leg is at most about 0.14 %/yr, and the computed margins are the better estimate.
3. Two rounding slips: v3 at 250k, 2000–2026 is 12.65 %, so 12.7 % not 12.6 %. v4's published-84 CAGR since 2000 is 18.65 %, so 18.7 % not 18.6 %.

**Comparing with the published backtest (added reference, not a correction)**
Comparing the retail results with the published 84-market figures mixes two effects. Most of the drop comes from removing the ethanol and iron-ore markets (CUA1 / SCO1) and the half-day lag, not from the small subsets or the real costs. On the 82 tradable markets with the half-day lag, the Sharpe since 2000 / since 2010 is:

| Variant | Since 2000 | Since 2010 |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | 0.28 | −0.02 |
| v2 | 0.55 | 0.27 |
| v3 | 0.63 | 0.32 |
| v4 | 0.69 | 0.36 |
| v5 | 0.72 | 0.375 |

The retail v5 since 2010 is 0.40 / 0.42 / 0.38 at 100k / 250k / 1M, about the same as that reference. These figures are in reference_84_vs_82lag.csv. For v5 they match the audit's restatement exactly (1.074 / 0.723 / 0.375).

**series_variantes.pkl and the forward step**
- It contains what the forward Monte Carlo needs: 7,180 days × 15 columns, with no NaN or inf values, on the same dates as cv_avant_impot/series.pkl from 1999-01-04. The stats give volatility, Sharpe and mean margin as a fraction. A 500-path smoke test through mc_engine.sim_diy runs for all 15 columns.
- One trap: the series start in 1999. If it is joined onto the 1990-start window that 04_final uses (D90), you get 2,350 NaN rows and the shocks come out entirely NaN. Use the 1999+ sample.
- The stats compute Sharpe and vol ×16, while mc_engine uses 261 days a year, a difference of about 1 %.

**Extreme days are real, not data errors**
- v1's −30 to −35 % days in Oct–Dec 2008 are broad losses caused by its fixed sizing.
- v5's big rate-driven days are real events: 3 Dec 2015 (Euribor ER4 and the German Schatz DU1, held at about 24× and 14× capital) and 13 Mar 2023 (SOFR, SFR5).

**Caveat to state in the report**
All past figures are for a USD account: US T-bill cash, USD returns. The forward step is in EUR (€STR). For a EUR-based investor, excess return and Sharpe are essentially unchanged. But IBKR's EUR benchmark minus 0.5 % was zero or below from about 2012 to mid-2022, so cash interest would have been about zero. That probably lowers the all-fee CAGR since 2010 by roughly 0.5 point a year. I could not compute this: there is no euro short-rate series in the data and the ECB data site is blocked by the network proxy.

futur.summary:
I ran the forward Monte Carlo for all 5 variants at USD 100k, 250k and 1M, net of all fees, over 10 and 5 years. Variant 5 reproduces the audit's 10-year central medians: 3.34 / 4.58 / 5.36 % against 3.28 / 4.61 / 5.41 %, differences of +0.06 / −0.03 / −0.05 pt, so the ±0.15 check passes. Everything is in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-snt-2b-adam-cieniewicz/4246b01c-1857-5934-aed2-b3eb85d88a07/scratchpad/audit/var_futur/ (scripts 01_params.py to 04_anchor_se.py). Nothing under /home/user/snt-2b-adam-cieniewicz was changed; git status is clean.

**Method.** The method is the same as the verified variant-5 run.
- Engine: a copy of cv_avant_impot/mc_engine.py, `sim_diy` in 'ibkr' mode, called with the same settings as the verified run.
- Simulation: stationary bootstrap with a mean block of 126 days, 4 seeds (101 / 202 / 303 / 404) × 10,000 paths. €STR is 2.4 %, inflation 2 %, fixed costs USD 400 a year.
- Cash: margin earns nothing; IBKR pays €STR − 0.5 % on cash above USD 10k, pro rata below 100k NAV; the rest sits in a money-market fund at €STR − 0.12 %.
- Shocks: each variant × tier's own daily series from series_variantes.pkl (1999-01-04 to 2026-07-10), standardised. Within a seed every key uses the same bootstrap indices, so differences between variants are not seed noise.
- Vol: each series' realised vol since 2000 (×16): about 39 / 37 / 35 % for v1 and 19.5 to 22 % for v2–v5.
- Margin: 17 % for variant 5, scaled for the other variants by published gross exposure: 10.2 / 10.8 / 13.1 / 15.1 / 17.0 %.
- Cash kept at IBKR: margin plus 23 % × vol / vol(v5). This gives 40 % for v5; for the other variants it is my assumption.

**Forward Sharpe rule.**
- Anchor A = each variant's realistic retail Sharpe since 2010 at that tier (half-day lag, whole contracts, real IBKR costs, ×16):
  - v1: 0.07 / −0.01 / 0.01
  - v2: 0.25 / 0.29 / 0.26
  - v3: 0.28 / 0.37 / 0.32
  - v4: 0.39 / 0.39 / 0.37
  - v5: 0.40 / 0.42 / 0.38
- Haircut h(tier) = v5 central / A(v5) = 0.499 / 0.577 / 0.717 (100k / 250k / 1M).
- Case 1 (common haircut): central Sharpe = h × A.
- Case 2: v1 and v2 lose only the decay part, taken as 75 % of their own haircut in Sharpe units, so central = A × (0.25 + 0.75 h). v3 to v5 are unchanged.
- Pessimistic and optimistic = central ∓ 0.20.

**Which case is central.** I treat case 2 as central for v1 and v2, and case 1 as their conservative bound. The audit's haircut on variant 5 explicitly includes a cut for picking it after seeing the results (it was the best of 53 variants tested). That cut cannot apply to rules fixed before the results were known. The 75/25 split is if anything generous to the decay share, since the audit's own 25–35 % selection cut implies a larger selection share. In practice the choice only moves v2, by +0.4 to +0.7 pt.

- v1 in case 1 gives −5.6 / −6.0 / −4.1 %.
- Pessimistic / optimistic medians over 10 years:
  - v1: −12.8 / 2.8, −13.0 / 1.4, −10.5 / 2.9 %
  - v2: −1.8 / 6.9, −0.4 / 7.8, −0.3 / 8.3 %
  - v3: −2.7 / 6.7, −0.4 / 8.3, 0.0 / 8.9 %

  - v5: −1.2 / 8.0, 0.1 / 9.2, 0.9 / 10.0 %
- Each +0.1 of forward Sharpe adds about 2.0 to 2.3 pt a year to the median for v2–v5, and 3.4 to 3.9 pt for v1.

**5-year central medians.**
- v1: −5.3 / −6.3 / −4.2 %
- v2: 2.3 / 3.4 / 3.8 %
- v3: 1.8 / 3.8 / 4.3 %
- v4: 3.3 / 4.3 / 5.3 %
- v5: 3.3 / 4.6 / 5.3 %
- P(loss) after 5 years: v1 64–69 %, v2 33–38 %, v3 32–42 %, v4 29–35 %, v5 29–36 %.

**Past versus expected.** Past figures are the verified retail simulation, net of all fees, USD account (100k / 250k / 1M).

| Variant | Past 2000–26 | Past 2010–26 | Expected, 10-year median |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | 0.5 / 3.0 / 4.4 % | −2.8 / −4.2 / −2.5 % | −5.2 / −6.1 / −4.0 % |
| v2 | 7.7 / 10.6 / 11.1 % | 3.6 / 4.6 / 4.3 % | 2.5 / 3.6 / 3.9 % |
| v3 | 9.0 / 12.7 / 13.1 % | 4.4 / 6.4 / 5.6 % | 1.9 / 3.9 / 4.4 % |
| v4 | 10.6 / 13.6 / 13.3 % | 6.9 / 7.2 / 6.9 % | 3.3 / 4.2 / 5.3 % |
| v5 | 11.2 / 14.7 / 15.1 % | 7.2 / 7.9 / 7.1 % | 3.3 / 4.6 / 5.4 % |

For comparison, from the verified audit run (10-year medians): euro money-market fund 2.3 %, trend ETF 4.7 % (10th percentile 0.1 %), 100 % Nasdaq-100 (QQQ-type) 5.9 % (10th percentile −5.1 %), 70 % Nasdaq-100 + 30 % trend ETF 6.4 %, 100 % S&P 500 6.0 %.

**What this means.**
- Variants 2 to 5 have a 10-year median of only 1.9 to 5.4 %, roughly the trend ETF's 4.7 %. The chance of doing worse than the money-market fund is 33 to 52 %, and the median worst drawdown is 41 to 46 %.
- Variant 1 is expected to lose money: about −4 to −6 % a year at the median. Its 35–39 % volatility costs about 7 pt a year of compounding, and it falls to 60 % of the starting capital in about 3 paths out of 4.
- The ranking of v2 to v5 is inherited from anchors that are not statistically distinct. Since 2010, v5 beats v2 by 0.11 to 0.15 of Sharpe, which is about 1 standard error (t = 1.0 to 1.2). It beats v4 by 0.004 to 0.024 (t = 0.1 to 0.3). Only v1 is clearly worse (t = 1.8 to 2.3). This is why v4 and v5 come out almost identical at 100k and 1M.

**Robustness.**
- The standard deviation of the median across seeds is 0.03 to 0.12 pt.
- Using margin computed on actual contracts instead of the gross-exposure scaling changes medians by −0.19 to +0.11 pt.
- Variant 5's tails are a little narrower than in the audit. At 100k / 250k / 1M the 10th percentile is −4.55 / −4.41 / −3.31 % against −5.05 / −4.48 / −3.96 %. P(loss) is 30.0 / 26.1 / 21.9 % against 31.1 / 26.0 / 23.3 %. The worst-decile drawdown is −62.8 / −65.5 / −62.5 % against −65.3 / −66.2 / −65.4 %. This is because the shocks now come from each portfolio's own retail series starting in 1999, while the audit's sub-portfolio series started in 1990.

caveats: The forward Sharpe rule has two weak points. First, it calibrates the haircut only on variant 5 (0.20 / 0.24 / 0.27 from the audit) and applies the same ratio to every variant. Second, the anchors since 2010 have a standard error of about 0.25 each. The v2–v5 differences are about 1 standard error or less (v5 vs v4: t = 0.1 to 0.3), so the ranking of the forward medians among v2–v5 is weakly supported. Only v1's shortfall is fairly robust (t = 1.8 to 2.3).

The 75 % decay / 25 % selection split for case 2 is an assumption from the task. The audit's own description of the cut for picking the variant after the fact (25–35 % of the Sharpe) implies a larger selection share, so case 2 may still be conservative for v2. For a negative anchor (v1 at 250k, A = −0.014) the multiplicative rule is backwards: case 2 gives −0.0098 against −0.0083 in case 1. This is immaterial.

Pessimistic and optimistic are central ∓0.20 as specified. For variant 5 this gives 0.00 / 0.04 / 0.07 and 0.40 / 0.44 / 0.47, against the audit's 0.00 / 0.03 / 0.05 and 0.40 / 0.43 / 0.47, so v5's pessimistic medians at 250k and 1M are about 0.1–0.4 pt higher than in the audit.

As the task specifies, margin for v1–v4 is 17 % × gross exposure / v5's gross exposure (published 84-market figures, 1990+). The verified past step showed this understates v1's margin (10 % against 17–18 % computed on contracts). The contract-margin sensitivity is reported and moves medians by −0.19 to +0.11 pt. Cash kept at IBKR = margin + 23 % × vol / vol(v5) is my assumption, since only v5's 40 % / 17 % was given. Moving 10 pts of NAV between IBKR cash and the money-market fund changes returns by about 0.04 pt/yr.

Conventions: vol and Sharpe are ×16 (project convention) and are fed into an engine that annualises with 261 days. Simulated daily vol is therefore about 1 % below the series, and the drift about 2 % below the anchor. This is the same as the audit and is absorbed by the haircut calibrated on v5. CAGR is in calendar time.

Shocks are each portfolio's own retail daily series from 1999-01-04 to 2026-07-10 (7,180 days), standardised and resampled in blocks with a mean length of 126 days. They contain 2008 and the 2023–26 drawdown, not the 1990s. For variant 5 this gives slightly thinner tails than the audit's 1990+ sub-portfolio series: 10th percentile 0.1–0.6 pt higher, 90th percentile 0.2–0.9 pt lower, worst-decile drawdown 0.7–2.9 pts milder. The same probably applies to the other variants, which the audit did not run.

The simulation keeps trading after any loss: there is no stop rule, and P&L is proportional to NAV. Whole contracts make that only approximate. After a 40 % drawdown at 100k several markets would fall below one contract, and an investor in v1, which touches 60 % of capital in 69–77 % of paths, would very likely stop. v1's negative median comes mainly from volatility drag at 35–39 % vol (about 7 pt a year), not from its Sharpe.

Past figures are for a USD account with US T-bill cash. Forward figures are EUR returns at €STR 2.4 %, with IBKR's USD 10k and 100k thresholds applied in USD-equivalent wealth. The verified past step estimated, without computing it, that a EUR investor's past all-fee CAGR since 2010 would be about 0.5 pt a year lower, because IBKR's EUR cash rate was about zero from 2012 to 2022.

The reference rows (cash, trend ETF, S&P 500, Nasdaq-100, 70/30 mixes) are copied from the verified audit run (rendement_attendu_10ans_ib_gateway.csv, 4 × 10k paths, different shocks). They were not re-simulated here.

Market subsets, contract sizes and spreads are today's, as in the past step (look-ahead in which markets are chosen, not in performance). Fixed costs are USD 400 a year at every tier, and the investor's own time is not counted. The forward results inherit every approximation of the retail series: half-day lag as a 50/50 mix, micro contracts assumed available throughout, and spreads before 2010 probably understated.
